meta.title: Research studio R4: data you can defend (the studio's own text)
meta.note: The numbers on this page are computed in the browser from b02-python-data.json (SPP 2025, EIA-930, before cleaning). The cleaning rules are the course's own documented example (the data build behind town_year.json). Licence facts were checked on the dates given in sources.

predict.q: Which number will your cleaning move most, in percent of its raw value? (The peak's clock time is a label: step 6 checks it apart.)

time.label: Time base
time.q: How does your study keep time?

options.label: Keep the UTC rows; label results in Central time with daylight saving
options.log: Rows kept in UTC, hour ending, as EIA publishes them; results labelled in U.S. Central time with daylight saving.
options.note: The rows never move, so no hour is lost or doubled; only the labels follow the local clock.

options.label: Keep the UTC rows and report in UTC
options.log: Rows kept in UTC, hour ending; results labelled in UTC.
options.note: Defensible if every table says UTC, but a reader in Kansas will take a 21:00 peak for an evening one.

options.label: Shift to Central Standard Time (UTC−6) all year
options.log: Rows labelled in Central Standard Time (UTC−6) all year; no daylight saving.
options.note: Every day has 24 rows, but summer labels run one hour behind the local clock. Say so in the note.

options.label: Shift to the local clock and force every day to 24 rows
options.log: Rows put on the local clock; 9 March padded with a copied hour and one of the two 01:00 hours of 2 November dropped, so every day has 24 rows.
options.note: Two hours are now wrong, yet the file still has 8,760 rows, so a row check passes. Only the log shows it.

options.label: Flag demand under half the median (the course's rule)
options.log: Demand under half the median ({limit} MW) flagged as implausible (provisional: to check against the operator's records).
options.note: Under a tenth of the hours around it, then back an hour later: far more likely a reporting error than a real event. Flag it provisionally; check the operator's records.

options.label: Flag demand more than 3 standard deviations below the mean
options.log: Demand more than 3 standard deviations below the mean (under {limit} MW) flagged as implausible (provisional: to check against the operator's records).
options.note: A different rule finds the same single hour. Two rules agreeing makes the flag more convincing, not proven.

options.label: Keep every value
options.log: No spike rule: every demand value kept.
options.note: The one suspect hour becomes the year's lowest demand, and any study of minimum load inherits it.

frozen.label: Frozen-reading rule
frozen.q: How many identical readings in a row make a suspected stuck feed?

options.label: 3 hours (the course's rule)
options.log: Runs of 3 or more identical non-zero readings flagged as suspected frozen telemetry.
options.note: The course's data build uses 3; your counts now match it. That shows consistency with the build, not that every flag is right.

options.label: 2 hours
options.log: Runs of 2 or more identical non-zero readings flagged as suspected frozen telemetry.
options.note: Catches more, but a healthy feed can repeat a value for two hours by chance: more false alarms.

options.label: 4 hours
options.log: Runs of 4 or more identical non-zero readings flagged as suspected frozen telemetry.
options.note: Fewer false alarms; short repeated runs remain unflagged.

options.label: 6 hours
options.log: Runs of 6 or more identical non-zero readings flagged as suspected frozen telemetry.
options.note: Fewer false alarms; more short repeated runs remain unflagged.

options.label: 12 hours
options.log: Runs of 12 or more identical non-zero readings flagged as suspected frozen telemetry.
options.note: A trade-off, not a verdict: runs shorter than 12 hours stay unflagged, so fewer false alarms and more missed freezes. Say why in your note.

options.label: 24 hours
options.log: Runs of 24 or more identical non-zero readings flagged as suspected frozen telemetry.
options.note: Fewest false alarms, most missed freezes: runs shorter than 24 hours stay unflagged. Say why in your note.

options.label: Off
options.note: Every stuck reading counts as real, including the December week.

fill.label: Fill method
fill.q: What happens to the flagged hours?

options.label: Use the same hour on nearby valid days (the course's rule)
options.log: Flagged values filled with the mean of the same UTC hour (rows 24 apart) on valid days within 7, then 21, then 45 days.
options.note: Keeps the daily shape, give or take an hour near the daylight-saving changes. It borrows other days' weather and can copy bad night readings: check solar at night.

options.label: Draw a straight line across each gap
options.log: Flagged values filled with straight lines between the valid hours either side.
options.note: Fine for an hour or two; across a week-long freeze it erases every daily cycle.

options.label: Leave the flagged hours out
options.log: Flagged values left out of every total.
options.note: Annual totals now add up fewer hours, so the year's energy is understated.

spatial.context: Your study adds wind-turbine locations from the U.S. Wind Turbine Database for Prairie Town's county (illustrative). The file stores latitude and longitude in degrees ([[epsg-code|EPSG:4326]]).
spatial.systems: The projected options: [[utm|UTM]] zones keep distances close to true locally; [[web-mercator|Web Mercator]] is for showing web maps; [[equal-area-projection|equal-area Albers]] keeps areas true across the contiguous U.S.

questions.q: Which coordinate system for 1 km setback buffers (the zone within 1 km of each turbine)?

why.deg: A degree is not a fixed distance: a buffer in degrees is not 1 km.
why.web: [[web-mercator|Web Mercator]] is for showing maps; it stretches distances.
why.utm: Right: a local projected system in metres, such as the county's [[utm|UTM]] zone, keeps distances close to true.

questions.q: And for the area the 1 km buffers cover, in square kilometres?

why.web: Web Mercator inflates areas away from the equator.
why.alb: Right: an equal-area system for the contiguous United States keeps areas true.
why.utm: Close for one county, but the safe rule for areas is an equal-area system.

spatial.log: Spatial layer (proposed, not yet processed): U.S. Wind Turbine Database v9.1 (public domain; acknowledgment kept). Coordinate systems chosen: {buffer} for the 1 km buffers; {area} for areas. Input file, outputs and counts to log when you run it.

note_fields.label: Known limits
note_fields.hint: For example: filled hours borrow other days' weather; solar still fails the night check; the spike rule cannot catch a plausible wrong value.

note_fields.label: How to rerun
note_fields.hint: The notebook or script, its settings and the expected four numbers.

practice.task: Open the starter notebook with the raw file next to it; reproduce the page's four numbers, then your own choices.
Read the sensitivity table for your choices; add a night rule for solar, rerun the night check and log both.
Spatial layer in QGIS: Ford County, Kansas, from the U.S. Wind Turbine Database; reproject for 1 km buffers and for area, each step logged (notebook part 3).
Check the licence of every source you use and write its attribution line.
Write the data note; ask someone to rerun your numbers from it alone.

rubric.look: Every cleaning step is logged with its rule, count, reason and effect, so another person can rerun it from the note alone. R4 covers this audit trail; R5 adds the verification log and validation.
The licence of every source is checked and stated, with the attribution lines it asks for.
